item.research_question: How does the number of principal elements (N) in equimolar multi-principal element alloys affect the probability of forming disordered solid solution (SS) phases versus intermetallic (IM) phases, and what are the implications for high-temperature structural applications?
item.material_system: Equimolar combinations of 3 to 6 elements from a palette of 26 metallic elements (including Al, Si, Mo, Ta, W, Nb, Ti, V, Re, Zr, Cr, Fe, Co, Ni, etc.)
item.processing_route: High-throughput computational screening using the CALPHAD method (Pandat v.8.1 software) to calculate phase diagrams for 134,547 equimolar alloy systems; results filtered for credibility where the fraction of fully assessed binary systems (fAB) equals 1.
item.test_conditions: Phase diagrams calculated between 600 °C and 3,600 °C; properties evaluated at the solidus temperature (Tm) and at 600 °C; maximum use temperature (Tuse) estimated as the lowest of 0.8Tm or the last first-order phase reaction temperature below Tm.
key_findings: The fraction of solid solution (SS) alloys decreases as the number of elements (N) increases: at Tm, 30% of 3-component alloys are SS, dropping to only 5% for 6-component alloys.
Configurational entropy rises slowly with N (as ln(N)), while the number of binary interactions increases rapidly (as (N/2)(N−1)), explaining why IM formation becomes more probable as N increases.
The maximum solidus temperature (Tm) decreases with N: 2,925 °C for 3-component, 2,754 °C for 4-component, 2,435 °C for 5-component, and 2,056 °C for 6-component alloys.
The maximum maximum use temperature (Tuse) decreases with N: 2,285 °C for 3-component, 1,846 °C for 4-component, 1,677 °C for 5-component, and 1,159 °C for 6-component alloys.
Only 3 out of 209 SS alloys with Tuse ≥ 1,000 °C are 6-component alloys, whereas 108 are 3-component alloys.
Extreme property values (highest/lowest density, modulus, cost) are achieved in ternary (3-component) alloys, while 6-component alloys show tighter property spreads.
51 equimolar alloy systems with 3 ≤ N ≤ 5 were identified that satisfy aggressive design criteria (Tuse ≥ 1,000 °C, density ≤ 10 g cm−3, modulus ≥ 100 GPa, cost ≤ $200/kg, no IM phases at Tm).
item.mechanism: The authors argue that while configurational entropy (Smix) favors solid solution stability, it increases only logarithmically with the number of elements. Conversely, the number of binary element pairs increases quadratically, raising the probability that at least one pair has a sufficiently large negative formation enthalpy (Hf) to overcome the entropy term in the Gibbs free energy equation (G = H - TS), thereby stabilizing intermetallic phases.
item.limitations: The study is restricted to equimolar compositions; non-equimolar alloys were not explored and may offer higher Tm or Tuse values. Additionally, the credibility filter (fAB=1) excluded over 95% of the calculated systems, potentially missing viable alloys if less stringent criteria were acceptable.
item.future_work: The authors propose extending the screening to non-equimolar alloys to uncover local compositions with extreme properties, conducting more extensive experimental validations to potentially relax credibility criteria, and developing high-throughput experimental techniques capable of handling microstructural length scales.
quotes: We find the surprising result that solid solution alloys become less likely as the number of alloy elements increases.

As the number of elements increases, the configurational entropy rises slowly while the probability of at least one pair of elements favouring formation of intermetallic compounds increases more rapidly.

The fraction of SS alloys noticeably decreases with an increase in the number of alloying elements, which can be understood by the competition between configurational entropy (favouring SS) and formation enthalpies (favouring IM phases).
